prompt.content: My neighbour grows soy every season on his field, is that a problem?

chosen.content: Growing soybean on the same plot for more than two consecutive years raises parasite pressure, so it is not advisable. You should first sow certified seed that is treated against damping-off. After sowing, weed the field at two weeks and repeat the weeding three weeks later. When you reach harvest, cut the stems at ground level and leave the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil. After the soybean crop, always follow with a cereal to capture the nitrogen contributed by the legume. For certified seed, consult ICAT/Sotouboua seed farm.

rejected.content: Growing soybean on the same plot for more than two years is not allowed, and you should not grow soybean on the same plot for more than three years consecutively. Soybean must be grown on land that has been rotated with cereal crops before you plant soybean again. After you finish soybean, you should plant a cereal crop to benefit from the nitrogen left by the soybean residues. If you need advice on soybean seed selection or the proper rotation, contact ICAT.

prompt.content: I notice dead central shoots in my maize, window-pane holes on the whorl leaves, and tunnels with frass inside the stems.

After the maize harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume like cowpea or soybean. If a large area of maize is affected, contact ICAT quickly for approved control.

prompt.content: My goats eat a lot of straw but it seems not enough in the dry saeson. What should I do with the harvest leftovers?

prompt.content: The old leaves on my maize are yellowing while the tops stay green, and the plants are short. What's the reason and what steps should I follow?

chosen.content: The older leaves of your maize become yellow because the plant moves nitrogen up to the younger leaves. First, look at the leaves before buying inputs; the uniform pale yellow on the lower, older leaves indicates nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often fails on run-down soil. Third, bring back organic matter by adding manure, compost, or burying residues instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, contact ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

prompt.content: The sheep in my pen are losing their wool and seem to have a dry mouth, could it be bloat?

prompt.content: my maize has yellow old leaves after heavy rain, it's nitrogen washout right?

chosen.content: It is not nitrogen washout. The two are told apart by timing: washout follows a heavy rain event, the nitrogen shortage shows a uniform pale yellowing of older leaves that worsens each season. Because it is a soil nitrogen shortage, you should read the leaves before buying anything, avoid broad-spectrum NPK and fungicide, bring organic matter back with manure, compost or unburnt residues, and add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation, cutting stems at ground level. Because it is nitrogen loss, you should open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing, and after the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burning. prompt.content: Why does my neighbour say 25% of maize fields get no yield boost from fertilizer?

Finally, take a soil sample to ICAT for analysis and the proper dose for your plot.

First, confirm the location gets 1,200-2,000 mm of rain each year and that the soil is deep, rich and drains well, at least 80-100 cm deep. Secure long-term rights to the land. Start with provisional banana shade, then establish permanent agroforestry shade at 12 m by 10 m spacing, about 90 trees per hectare. Plant seedlings in June or July. prompt.content: What fertiliser program should I use for maize in the Kara region?

chosen.content: In the Plateaux region the maize fertiliser programme uses only the standard doses, with no extra regional complement. First, after sowing, place four bags of NPK 15-15-15 (200 kg per hectare) in a pocket 5-10 cm from each seedling, waiting 10-15 days and ensuring the bag does not touch the plant. Then, at panicle initiation about 30-45 days after sowing, apply urea as a top-dress at 100 kg per hectare. No additional potash or phosphate is added for Plateaux. Finally, have ICAT verify the plan for any soil-specific adjustment.

Plant a resistant improved 55-75 day variety in the Kara region and do the first weeding at the right time. If you need help choosing a variety or dealing with a pest, go to ICAT.

prompt.content: My neighbour says I can just drop yam cuttings straight into the ground, is that right?

chosen.content: Use healthy yam seed setts, cut the faces, let them heal in shade and dust them with wood ash before you plant. First choose a deep, rested, stone-free soil that has been left fallow for at least five years, or use a brief Mucuna fallow if the plot is limited. Then make mounds 40-80 cm high, arranging them 1.4 x 1.4 m on rich soil to obtain about 5,000 mounds per hectare. Place the ash-covered yam seed setts on the mounds, stake the vines and perform the first weeding on time. Plant early yam varieties between November and March and acquire a good-storage variety such as TDr 747 or Florido from ICAT or ITRA.

First shape the bunches into an inverted pyramid with the base 30 to 60 cm wide and the stack 20 to 40 cm high, placing them on a rammed or cemented pit that is 80 cm by 80 cm, which gives about 10,000 yam per hectare. Before planting, clear the field of weeds and use a resistant, moderately vigorous variety that is suited for the region's rainfall. Plant the seedlings in rows spaced 50 by 50 cm, making sure each seedling has at least four buds. prompt.content: I have some brewery grain and fish meal, what else do I need for a proper boar feed?

chosen.content: A proper pig feed must contain three groups of ingredients. Combine energy sources such as maize, sorghum, cassava or yam and their peelings, brans and brewery grains with the protein sources you already have, like fish meal, adding soybean, groundnut cake and a little cottonseed or palm-kernel cake if you wish. Finish the mix with minerals and salt. Offer clean water at all times and let the pigs drink whenever they like. Boil any restaurant scraps before you add them to the feed to avoid disease. Increase the feed amount as the pigs grow. Give iron to piglets in the first days of life. For a costed ration and piglet iron or deworming details, consult a veterinary or extension officer.

rejected.content: A proper boar feed must contain three groups of ingredients: energy from the brewery grain and fish meal, protein from the legume such as cowpea or groundnut, and minerals and salt. Start by mixing roughly 50 kg of energy grains or brewery grains with a 100 kg of bone or mineral powder to create the energy portion. Then combine that with the legume mix, adding an extra 25 kg of minerals or salt per 100 kg of mixture. Finally, crush and mix the blend thoroughly before giving it to the boar. Always ensure the mixture is well-dense so it can be easily chewed and swallowed. If the boar appears weak or shows signs of bloat, consult a veterinary auxiliary.

Burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter, then disinfect the house. prompt.content: What are the basic parts of a swine pen to keep them healthy and tidy?

Construct the walls with banco for local breeds or cement bricks for improved ones. Put the pen on a rammed or cemented floor that you can clean and disinfect easily. Install the footbath right at the entrance and never let the pigs foul the pen without control. Finally, have an extension officer size the pens according to your herd size.

Ensure the pigs never touch water sources, food scraps and garbage. Maintain the pen in a clean state by replacing litter and disinfecting it regularly. Finally, notify the veterinary service right away if you see swiftness, bloat or any signs of African swine fever.

While the plants are still young, drop a pinch of this mixture into each whorl funnel where the borer larvae are feeding. One kilogram of the mixture will treat about 1,500 to 2,000 plants. If a large block is attacked at once, go to ICAT for approved control.

If the infestation is heavy, apply an approved insecticide at the labelled rate. I cannot give you the exact dosage or any chemical name, but ICAT and ITRA can provide the correct product and dosage for your situation.

prompt.content: Why do I need to hold part of my grain past the harvest glut?

Compare the local price plus transport costs with the price you could get in Lomé or other large urban markets. If possible, sell as a group or through a cooperative to reach bigger buyers and reduce per-bag transport cost. prompt.content: The leaves of my rice field have strange spindle spots with grey in the middle and dark outlines, and I see some neck damage.

chosen.content: Those signs indicate rice blast, which is caused by the fungus Pyricularia. First step is to stop over-applying nitrogen: split your urea applications and do not exceed the recommended amount. Then, treat the seed you will sow next season with a Fongorene-type seed treatment at six grams per kilogram of seed. If the blast outbreak is severe, use an approved benomyl-type fungicide at roughly five hundred grams per hectare, improve drainage and airflow in the field, and select a blast-tolerant rice variety. To have the disease confirmed and to receive the current approved fungicide and exact rate, consult ICAT.

prompt.content: I have a small plot, only 0.25 hectare, growing sorghum. How much fertilizer should I use?

chosen.content: You should put 37.5-50 kg of NPK and 12.5-25 kg of urea on your quarter-hectare sorghum field. First finish weeding, then spread the NPK at the rate of 150-200 kg per hectare, which equals the 37.5-50 kg you need. After that, apply the urea at 50-100 kg per hectare, giving the 12.5-25 kg amount. Plant the seed on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains in each pocket about three to five centimetres deep using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Thin the seedlings to two or three plants per pocket when they are two to three weeks old and do the first weeding without breaking the ridges. Protect the maturing panicles from birds and pull any Striga before it flowers. For advice on matching a sorghum variety to your local rains, go to ICAT.

rejected.content: You should put about 100 kg of fertilizer in your 0.25 ha field. First, choose a deep, rested, stone-free soil that is at least 80-100 cm thick and that has been fallow for at least five years. Use the improved durum variety that fits your area and stage of maturity. Apply the fertilizer at panicle initiation, which is 30-45 days after sowing. Keep the seed on the plot evenly spaced according to the variety's recommendation. If you need a variety that fits your region and stage, contact ICAT.

prompt.content: I have a small herd of local pigs and a muddy area near my house. I want to keep the boar separate from the sows and the young ones. What should I do?

chosen.content: Four compartments are needed so breeding and health are managed and disease does not run through the lot. Separate the boar, the sows, a nursing sow, and the weaned young to keep each group apart. Use banco for local breeds or cement bricks for improved ones, always on a rammed or cemented floor you can clean and disinfect. Build walls about 1.2 m high, add an exercise area, and put a footbath at the entrance to stop pigs from fouling the pen uncontrolled. An extension officer can help you size the pen for your herd.

rejected.content: Keep the boar away from the sows and the young ones until they reach about 3 months of age. Raise the boar with a mother sow in the shade of a robust cow, ensuring good feed and clean water for them. Maintain a constant supply of clean water and let the pigs drink freely whenever they wish. Avoid overcrowding the boar, because loose pigs can attack them. If the pigs become aggressive, contact the veterinary service immediately.

prompt.content: Assisted natural regeneration means I buy seedlings and plant them out every year, right?

chosen.content: No, and that is the useful part of it: it costs you no seedlings. The catalogue defines it as selecting and protecting the valuable young plants that grow in the field, in such a way that the field is never left bare. The plants are already coming up on their own. Your work is to choose them and keep them alive. The four steps are: know the area of your field, count the kinds of tree to protect, select the trees to protect, then protect and maintain the ones you kept. Maintaining them means weeding, fire breaks, a stake for the ones that are not vigorous, taking off the greedy branches, and keeping animals away. In the dry savanna zone the catalogue suggests keeping about 25 to 30 adult stems per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare.

rejected.content: Not at all. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is clear on what it is and what it is not: selecting and protecting the valuable young plants that come up on their own in a field, so you have less planting to do and less seed to buy. Its four steps are choosing the zones, selecting the pockets, protecting the plants and pulling the trees. The work is done in the season the field is usable, that is in June-July for the main crop, so the first weeding cannot start until the second season.

prompt.content: Every year the wind comes through and flattens part of my maize before harvest. My field is open on that side, nothing stops it.

chosen.content: What you are describing is what a windbreak is for. The catalogue defines it as a barrier, most often a curtain of trees planted in lines, sometimes trees with a taproot, standing against the dominant winds. It has two sides, the windward side that takes the wind and the sheltered side behind it. So: orient your line opposite to the direction the dominant wind comes from, which is the open side you just described. On a single line, space the plants 1 to 1.5 m, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. If you want it stronger, plant a band of two or three lines, 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m inside the line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Plant at the rainy season, not now if the rains are finished. What I cannot tell you is how much of your maize it will save: the catalogue gives no figure for that, and I will not invent one.

rejected.content: You are facing a problem with wind erosion in your maize. The correct step is to rebuild the soil's organic matter first, then apply a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean, cutting the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. After that, protect the new crop from the wind by sowing it early and using a short, dense stand. Do not rely on any fertilizer or a broad-spectrum fungicide because they will not solve the erosion. Visit ICAT to have the soil analyzed and to get the proper fertilizer recommendation.

prompt.content: By what routes does disease get into a flock?

chosen.content: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names them: contact with sick animals, contact with soiled droppings and secretions, and contaminated material, which it details as farm equipment, a vehicle, and contaminated clothes and shoes. Against those routes it sets three principles. Separation: do not mix your animals with other farms', quarantine every newly bought bird, isolate the sick. Cleaning, which already removes a good part of the germs. And disinfection, which inactivates what the cleaning left.

rejected.content: Contaminated swill, dirty water, and a dirty needle are the three routes of infection. First, collect all food scraps and spoiled leftovers and keep them away from the clean water. Second, clean any dirty pots or pans before you mix the feed. Third, give the birds a proper vaccination with the La Sota or B1 strain in water or as eye-drops and repeat the dose according to the schedule. If you need help, the veterinary service or ITRA can guide you.

prompt.content: Compost is just waste left to rot. I do not see why I would go to the trouble of layers.

chosen.content: The layers are the method, so if you drop them you are not doing what the catalogue describes. The catalogue does define composting in a heap as laying plant and animal waste and debris in a heap in a shaded spot to turn them into an organic fertiliser, so you are right about the raw idea. But it then sets out an order, step by step: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure on that base, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well. And a layer of topsoil or well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator, with every layer watered as it goes down. And it says you will have more control over what goes in, because the material is chosen for you. A heap, on the other hand, is a place to see. A certain amount of materials, in a certain way, takes a certain time, and you must know the ages of your soil before you put it in. The catalogue gives you that time and the range of results: a compost is ready when it looks and smells like dark, rich soil, that is 2-3 months at most, and it is always a soil, not a bag.

prompt.content: It rained hard once last week and everyone in the village is sowing.

chosen.content: One hard rain is not the settled rains. The maize brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and the sowing fiche says plainly not to sow on a first isolated shower. Check the window for where you are: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, ask ANAMET what this season is doing before you follow your neighbours.

rejected.content: The practice of sowing immediately after a heavy rain is common in the south, including Maritime and Plateaux, because those areas receive two rainy seasons. First, check the local radio for the official forecast and follow its warnings. Second, prepare your plot ahead of the rains so you can plant the moment the rains are truly established. Third, in the south you typically have one rainy season from roughly May to September, so do not sow on the first isolated shower. Finally, if you need help converting this seasonal outlook into a planting calendar, visit ICAT.

Whether your family can do it is arithmetic you can now do yourself: divide 420 by the number of people who will actually work, and see how that falls across the season. It will not fall evenly, because the days are bunched: 110 of them are harvest and transport for two hectares, 60 are the first weeding and thinning, 60 shelling and winnowing, 50 the second weeding. At 700 FCFA a man-day, 2005 prices, that labour alone is 294,000 FCFA. If the answer is no, hiring is a cost to put into the budget before you plant.

rejected.content: The catalogue gives no spacing between the rows, so I cannot tell you how many days your family will need to clear, how much land will have to be ploughed, how much earth moved, or how many bags of fertiliser to transport. What the catalogue does give is the sequence: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, mark it out with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, then carry out the work as a group on 8 to 10 days, with the help of a cooperative for the earth. So a second hectare needs 160 to 200 pegs, 2 to 3 days, and the work itself. ICAT can help you turn the plan into a work schedule, and the catalogue's brochure also gives the idea of a group working together.

prompt.content: The rains have stopped here. I have my windbreak plants ready and I am going to put them in tomorrow.

chosen.content: Hold them. The catalogue is explicit on this one point: the planting of the trees and shrubs that make up the windbreak must take place at the time of the rainy season. If your rains are finished, you would be putting young plants into ground that is about to dry out, and the catalogue gives you no way to compensate for that. Keep the plants and set them at the next rains. Use the time in between for the part that does not need water: work out the direction of the dominant wind, because you orient the line opposite to it, and measure the side you want to protect so you know your count. On a single line that is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m, and for a band of two or three lines 133 to 200 plants per 100 m.

rejected.content: The plants are meant to go in when the season is settled, which is when the rains actually start, not when they have stopped. Your order is in the sequence: determine the direction of the dominant wind, orient the plant lines opposite to it, set a first line 1 to 1.5 m wide, then a second line 2 m wider, with the plants set on their roots, and prune the plants to keep them short and dense. If you are in the south, remember that the plot for the plot season is chosen in July, against January for the sowing area. Ask ICAT what the reliable rains are this season.

prompt.content: Should I prepare my soil for one planting or two, but I haven't mentioned my location?

chosen.content: Soil preparation depends on the region among the five: Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, or Savanes. If you are in Kara or Savanes you will prepare for a single planting because the area is unimodal. If you are in Maritime or Plateaux you will prepare for two plantings because the area is bimodal. Centrale is a transition zone where either pattern may occur. Let me know your region to give the correct advice. For exact prefecture-level timing, consult ICAT.

prompt.content: Describe the trade I am making when I take a longer variety.

chosen.content: You are buying yield with time. Going from the short end of the list to the long, the potential yield rises from 3 tonnes a hectare to 7, and the average from 1.5 to 2 up to 3 to 4, while the cycle stretches from 75 to 85 days out to 105 to 115. What you are spending is rain you may not have: the extra thirty days have to be there at the end of the season, and if they are not, the crop is caught. The brochure puts it as weighing the cycle and the yield, which is exactly this trade. Obatanpa is worth noticing in the middle of it, 100 to 110 days with the highest average on the list, 3.5 to 4.

prompt.content: I have a small plot of about a quarter hectare on the Plateaux Ouest. The soil is deep and well-drained, and I can get rain of around 1,500 mm a year. I want to plant cacao in June-July and need shade. What steps should I follow?

chosen.content: First, confirm that your plot receives between 1,200 and 2,000 mm of rain annually, has rich, deep soil at least 80-100 cm deep, and that you have secured long-term land rights. Plant the cacao seedlings in June-July as the season advises. Immediately set up provisional shade using banana plants to shelter the young trees. After the provisional shade is in place, establish a permanent agroforestry shade grid spaced 12 metres by 10 metres; this spacing gives about 90 trees per hectare, which for your 0.25 ha field equals roughly 22 shade trees. Protect the apex of each cacao tree each month from psyllids and caterpillars and the base from termites, and create a firebreak before the dry season. For the best planting material and shade design, go to ICAT or ITRA.

chosen.content: Then you are already partway through the cycle and the next year is settled. Groundnut is a legume, one of the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen, which the catalogue puts in year one alongside beans and cowpea. So the year that follows it is maize, the hungry plant that takes a lot, sown now that the soil is rich in nitrogen. After that, year three is a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year four is an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to the legumes. The brochure's version of the same idea reads maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, so if you prefer a fallow to the okra year, that is in the sources too. prompt.content: I have a small plot of about a quarter hectare on the Plateaux Ouest. The soil is deep and well-drained, and I can get rain of around 1,500 mm a year. I want to plant cacao in June-July and need shade. What steps should I follow?

prompt.content: I have a small bag of cowpea from my field, some beans look a bit damp and a few are broken. What should I do before I store them?

chosen.content: First, sort the beans by removing all broken or discoloured ones, because damp grain moulds and undoes everything. Once the grain is fully dry, you can choose a storage method: mix an equal volume of sifted ash or fine sand through the grain in a tin, add a 3 cm ash layer on top and seal; or add 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil per 2.5 kg of grain, mix well and seal; or treat with an approved storage insecticide at the labelled dose and seal. For the correct insecticide product, contact ICAT.

Take a clean, dry storage bag and add the cowpea seeds alongside an equal amount of grain sorghum, millet or maize. Measure roughly 1.5 kg of the grain mix for every 20 kg of cowpea. Mix the cowpea and sorghum grain well so the seeds are well coated. After the mix is uniform, pack it tightly into the bag. Finally, seal the bag securely. For any questions about the approved storage product, contact ICAT.

prompt.content: My bunds slump and spread out after a few weeks.

chosen.content: Check the profile first and then the building. A main bund should be 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, and a secondary 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. A bund built with a narrow foot or straight sides has nothing to stand on and will spread. Then the method: water them as you build so they compact, which is the instruction people skip because it doubles the work at the time. A bund heaped dry and rained on afterwards settles into exactly what you describe. And leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, so the water leaves where you chose.

The catalogue advises that in the construction of your main bunds, the lower base is lowered: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base against 120 to 150 cm at the top, and that water is raised towards the ends of the main bund rather than at the top. And it gives exactly how it should be done, which is to leave openings towards the ends of the main bund to evacuate the water. The two other things to check are the orientation of the bunds, which should follow the slopes rather than a straight line, and the spillways on the roof, which the catalogue says to be opened against the rain.

prompt.content: Set out the pricing method and the market instructions.

chosen.content: The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference gives pricing as five steps: record every expense; work out the cost of production per head; decide the profit you want per head; compare that price with the market price; readjust if the market asks for it. On the market side it gives four instructions: look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after; keep a client register; sign contracts with them where you can; and honour what the contract says. Beside those it lists how to make the farm known: radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds, word of mouth and a signboard. The study names no buyer and gives no current price; its own figures, 2,250 FCFA a bird and 100 FCFA an egg, are 2020 evaluations used to build a projection.

Record every expense, work out your cost per head, compare that with the market price you decided, and readjust if the market asks for it. Sell as a group through a cooperative or with ICAT, and look for your buyers before the batch starts rather than after.

prompt.content: How big should the run be for sixty hens?

chosen.content: That figure is not in what I hold, so I will not size it for you. What the 2017 ESFT compendium gives is that there should be a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander, that a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and that hens should have a run where they can eat grass, failing which you bring them a little greenery every day. The densities I do have are for indoors: 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 50 chicks, 12 to 15 growers in the commercial reference, and 5 to 6 hens per square metre in the village one. Ask ICAT for the run, since it holds the plans.

rejected.content: Sixty hens need a run where they can eat, drink and breathe freely, with a space to move. Build the run with a wall of 0.5 to 1 m and include four pillars at 1.5 m. Place feeders and waterers along the sides of the run, not inside it. Cast a trough for drinking that is at least 1.5 m long, three metres wide and three metres deep, and place it away from the building. Give the hens a nest box of 0.5 m by 0.5 by 1 m and three of them. For the chick room, the 2020 reference gives fewer openings so the warmth stays in, and it raises the wall to 1.2 m.

prompt.content: I am going out to gather residues this morning. What am I looking for?

chosen.content: The fast rotting kind: straw, and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. Those are what the catalogue names for the main residue layer, and you chop them before they go in. Leave the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize where they are, and the husks too, because they rot slowly and are named as the ones to avoid there. While you are out, gather the other components as well, since the heap is not residues alone: a little wood ash, manure for the 5 cm layer, topsoil, and rice husks or ronier leaves for the 10 to 20 cm base. And make sure you can water, because each layer is watered as it is laid.

rejected.content: The stalks of sorghum, millet or maize, and a few other plants you can identify. The catalogue names straw, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and pattyams and yam, as residues that rot fast, and it advises against leaving them in the field too long. Straw is the first to go at the first cut, and the list also names chopped groundnut leaves, chopped soya leaves, and the husks as fast rotting material, with rice husks and ronier leaves among the other ways to keep them in the heap. Know which of the residues you are dealing with before you go to the field.

prompt.content: Should I follow the calendar date or wait for the rain?

chosen.content: Wait for the rain, and use the date as the frame. The maize brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and gives the windows: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. The calendar fiche explains why the rain wins: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. That is also why it sends you to ANAMET for this year's rains.

rejected.content: Wait for the rains to actually start, not the date, and prepare your plot beforehand. The north (Kara, Savanes) gets rain roughly May-September, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy seasons, and Centrale is transitional. Sow only after the rains are established, not after a single early shower. For turning this seasonal outlook into a planting plan, see ICAT. I cannot give you a live forecast or a day-ahead rain prediction.

prompt.content: My brother has disease in his flock and is asking me what to do.

chosen.content: Give him the six steps and tell him to start with the fourth if he only does one. Isolate the sick birds. Forbid any trading in his henhouse. Forbid any visit without a precise purpose. Inform the veterinary service of his locality quickly. Never eat the carcasses. Burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Tell him not to buy medicine on a guess, because no treatment cures a viral disease and medicines act only on the parasitic and bacterial ones. And do not go and see him yourself for now: the visit rule is there because disease travels on contaminated material, farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes, as well as on animals.

rejected.content: Tell him what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists for every illness and what to do with them, and give him the signs to watch for. Tell him to watch the birds for a fever, for discharge from the nose and the mouth, for discharge from the ears, for thyroid trouble, for hives, and for being off their feed and their drink. Tell him to isolate the sick birds or to take them out to treat them, and to inform the veterinary service of the location. Tell him not to visit other farms for that reason, and to call the veterinary service the same day for a diagnosis and a treatment. And tell him to keep the birds where they are, away from the rest, with their feed and their water clean, because they are not ill with a virus that survives in the food.

prompt.content: Just tell me the registers are optional if the farm is going well.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists them without conditions: visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out. Two things you lose by skipping them. You cannot set a price properly, because the method that reference gives starts with recording every expense and working out the cost of production per head. And when something does go wrong, you will have no history to show the animal health worker, at the moment you most need one. A few lines a week is the whole cost. If you want to argue the point with someone who can see your farm, ICAT is the place.

It is one of three lines of accounting: 2,150,491 FCFA of start-up, 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital, 2,376,785 FCFA of first year projection, and a first year net result of 131,785 FCFA on a profit of only 3,487,181 FCFA. The reason is stated in its own definition: a second year result is only possible if the first is real, and the first is real only if the second is well carried out. So the useful rows are the ones that fail to close: the investment side, where the houses, the tractor, the seed, the fertiliser and the man-days are listed in 2005 prices, and the first year working capital, where the small items are not priced. A second year is the first year in the study, so the gap between them is real and the failure point in the study is not.

prompt.content: I have no money for five compartments at once. Which do I build first?

chosen.content: Start with what the birds you actually have need. The five compartments of the 2020 commercial reference are the breeders with a shared yard, the brooding room, the chick room, and two grower compartments with a yard. If you begin with a breeding nucleus of sixty hens and six cocks, the breeder compartment and the chick room come first, since chicks must be kept apart and warm. Build the rest as the flock grows, and ask ICAT to help you stage it against your budget.

rejected.content: Start with the nucleus: breeder compartment, 4 m by 3.5 m, two bricks at most, 3 m high, for 60 birds. That is the compartment where the chicks spend their first three weeks, and it has fewer openings than the rest, which is what lets you close it against the wind and the rain. Then make the chick room of 50 birds, 4 m by 3 m and three bricks at most, low wall, 30 to 35 cm high, two bricks. Then the grower compartment, 7 m by 4 m, two bricks, high by high, three bricks, for 100 birds, with the chick room taken apart. Build the middle compartments only after the chicks are settled. For the breeder and chick room, the 2020 reference gives the same size ratio as the breeder compartment.

Sell the cockerels you do not need, which is part of flock management in the 2017 ESFT compendium, and keep the six best: vigorous, agile, with a well developed bright red comb.

One cock for ten hens is the minimum ratio the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives, and sixty hens call for more than one cock: at that size you have to hatch for other farmers as well, otherwise the unit does not pay for itself. The 2017 ESFT compendium says to buy breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and not to buy any from a market. Buying the wrong number of cocks offsets the whole plan. For the rest of your budget, the 2020 reference gives 3,850,124 FCFA for the houses, 2,150,491 for the equipment, 1,422,181 for the feed, and 200,000 for the first year's work, all in 2020 prices.

prompt.content: Set out the construction procedure.

chosen.content: Before construction: determine the slopes with a water level; draw the plan from them; mark the plan out on the site with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare. Construction: raise the bunds to profile, main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30; water them as they are built so that they compact. Openings: leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund to let excess water out. Organisation: the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation. Site: replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site.

rejected.content: On a shaded site, out of the wind and rain, for eight to ten days. Choose a fallow of at least five years first. Host: maize. Steps: Choose a fallow of at least five years first, because the striga tolerant maize and the grain fertiliser act together: the two are sown in the same season in the same field, and the fertiliser is put in at the first crop's centimeter. On the soil, measure 10 to 15 m between one hectare and two between one and three. Then determine the depths: 30 cm for the strong plants, 25 for the medium ones. Plant during the strong rains, not at the first shower. For the seed, visit ITRA or a registered distributor, who can tell you which variety suits your region this season.

prompt.content: Everything on my farm is the same age and the henhouse is empty half the year.

chosen.content: You are running one cycle where the model runs six. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year, which is why it asks for at least five compartments: a breeder compartment, a brooding compartment, a chick room and two grower compartments, all occupied at once by birds of different ages. Start staggering: set a batch of eggs, then another before the first leaves the brooder at three weeks, and so on. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs, and the brooder is meant to handle small hatchings in series, so the equipment already assumes this. Staggering also spreads your sales, which matters because you are meant to find buyers before each batch is ready. Write the settings and hatchings in the movement register so you can see the rhythm build.

rejected.content: Then the ratio is wrong. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference culls at 24 months and hens and cocks alike, and a henhouse that stays empty half the year means there are cocks around all year, which is exactly why it is culling at that age. The reason the reference does not give is that a henhouse kept open is what lets disease through, so a good cleaning is its own instruction, and it also keeps predators off. prompt.content: When is the best time of year to plant chili pepper in my garden?

chosen.content: The best time to plant chili pepper is when you have a water point and can grow year-round. Transplant vigorous seedlings that are 10 to 15 cm tall into rich, well-drained beds, spacing them 50 by 50 cm or 70 by 60 cm. Manage the nursery carefully and never water late in the evening to avoid damping-off. After transplanting, stake the plants, keep the beds weeded and earth up, and scout regularly for aphids, mites and fruit rot. Do not grow chili after tomato, eggplant or gboma because they share the same pests and diseases, so rotate onto cereal or legume land. I cannot give you an exact planting date, and you should ask ICAT for a suited variety and approved products.

rejected.content: You should grow chili pepper after tomato, eggplant or gboma and use 20-25 kg per hectare of treated improved seed. First, select a resistant variety that matures in 55-75 days. Then, transplant 20-25 cm seedlings at 50 x 50 cm or 70 x 60 cm spacing. Weed the plot at 15-25 days and again at 40 days. Apply NPK at 150-200 kg per hectare, then urea at 50-100 kg per hectare, and earth up against damping-off. Protect the seedlings from birds from flowering to harvest. For a variety suited to your area, see ICAT.

prompt.content: How much should I feed a bird that is sick and off its food?

chosen.content: That is not in what I hold and I will not improvise a sick bird's ration. The figures I have are for healthy birds by age: about 10 to 25 grams a day from 1 to 60 days, 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale at six months, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. Not eating is one of the eight signs of a sick bird, along with being sad, drowsy and downcast, drooping wings, feathers standing up, keeping away from the flock, thinness, discharge from the nose and the mouth, difficulty moving and diarrhoea. Isolate the bird or take it out, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Keep clean water in front of it whatever else you do.

rejected.content: Give it clean water at all times, because a shortage hits hens fast. Build a daily ration from four groups: energy from maize, sorghum, millet or brans; protein from cowpea, soy, oil cakes, fish meal, termites or maggots; and minerals/vitals from bone or shell powder and a supplement. Make sure the feeders and drinkers are never empty and wash them often. If the bird keeps refusing food, keeps drooling, or has a swollen throat, see the veterinary service.

prompt.content: How do I make compost using crop residues and animal manure?

chosen.content: Start a compost heap by alternating layers of crop residues, animal manure, and a little soil. Keep each layer damp like a wrung-out cloth. Turn the heap every few weeks. The compost is ready when it is dark, crumbly and no longer smells raw. Work the finished compost into the soil before sowing, aiming for about five tonnes per hectare, roughly fifty wheelbarrows. If you need a method suited to the residues you have, visit ICAT.

prompt.content: I moved north and everything I do seems to be at the wrong time.

chosen.content: You are probably still on the southern calendar, and the gap is about two months on every operation. In Maritime and Plateaux the plot is cleared in February and March, ploughed at the first rains in April and May, and sown when the rains are properly settled in April to May. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is cleared in April and May and ploughed and sown in June and July. That is because the south has two rainy seasons and the north one, around May to October. Ask ICAT for the calendar of your new prefecture, and follow ANAMET for this season's onset.

rejected.content: The north, covering Kara and Savanes, has one rainy season about May-September, so your southern crops such as maize are only in the south for one stretch. The south uses a bimodal system with two harvests a year, while the north uses a unimodal system with one harvest. You should sow at the start of the reliable rains, not after a single shower, and have your plot prepared in advance so you can sow the moment the rains are truly established. The north also has a single, longer dry spell, so plan for that later season. For exact dates with ANAMET, contact ICAT.

prompt.content: For a windbreak, single line or a band of several lines? Which do I take?

Band of two or three lines: 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m inside the line, which comes to 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. So the band costs you roughly twice the plants and takes more ground, and gives you a thicker barrier. In both cases you orient it opposite the dominant wind, and in both cases you plant at the rainy season. What the catalogue does not do is tell you which one protects better, or by how much. It gives no comparison and no figure. If your wind is strong and your plot is worth it, the band is the heavier answer; ICAT can look at your plot and say.

prompt.content: My bunds slump and spread out after a few weeks.

chosen.content: Check the profile first and then the building. A main bund should be 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, and a secondary 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. A bund built with a narrow foot or straight sides has nothing to stand on and will spread. Then the method: water them as you build so they compact, which is the instruction people skip because it doubles the work at the time. A bund heaped dry and rained on afterwards settles into exactly what you describe. And leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, so the water leaves where you chose.

rejected.content: That is what you are seeing, and the catalogue puts a name on it. The water is meant to move properly over the whole base, and the profile is what matters: the lower base at 30 cm, the main at 45 and the top at 60, watered so that it is never standing alone. A single opening between the main and the top, or a spillway meant to empty the upper bucket instead of the whole thing, will let the water run off the main part of the bund. That is not something to adjust in the weekend. Check the profile against the water you have: a water level across the whole bund before you start, which costs a few minutes, and water the bunds as you build so they compact.

rejected.content: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names the tarpaulins for the wind and rain, the gas incubator for keeping warm, the brooder for the chicks, the chick room, and the grower compartments for the growers. It lists the material for the tarpaulins, which are jute bags, and the tarpaulins as something you can make yourself. Tell me which of the four you are actually using, and I can give you a price on the parts you need to build.

prompt.content: I want to make compost but I have never done it.

Then start with the site rather than with the materials, because the catalogue treats the site as half the work: a shaded spot, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with a water point nearby as an advantage. Tell me what ground you have available and whether there is water near it, and tell me what residues you have on the farm, because some go in and some are kept out.
There is shade behind the house and the well is about thirty paces away. I have a lot of maize stalks and some groundnut leaves.

chosen.content: The site sounds right on all four counts, so take it. The residues are the problem: of your two, one goes in and one does not. The groundnut leaves are exactly what is wanted, named with straw and the leaves of soya and cowpea among the residues that rot fast, and you chop them before they go in. The maize stalks are on the other list, with the stalks of sorghum and millet and the husks, which rot slowly and are to be kept out of that layer. So gather more of the fast kind if you can, and ask ICAT what to do with the stalks instead, because the catalogue does not say. Then build in layers, watering each one as you lay it: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of your chopped leaves trodden down well, then a layer of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri, as the activator.

rejected.content: You have two things the catalogue wants you to have, both of which are easy to get: stalks of groundnut and maize and the leaves of cassava, soya or cowpea are not bad, and the slow rotting material, rice husks or ronier leaves, is exactly what the site is meant for, since the heap is intended to be a shaded site with a water point nearby as an advantage. So the first step is to turn those into something that stays in the heap for at least two months: the stalks and the leaves of groundnut and soya are the two the catalogue names for that, alongside the husks of maize, cowpea or soya and the husks of groundnut, cassava and yam. The manure, on the other hand, is not a material to put on top of that: the catalogue gives composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of raising a grower's income, and it names the birds as the income it is meant to help raise. Once the site is ready, the two things you have will be what you build: a little wood ash spread over the whole base, 10 to 20 cm thick, and the residues trodden down well.

The month bands are there as a frame, April to May in Maritime and Plateaux and June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, not as the decision. If they want something better than an argument, ANAMET gives this season's onset and its forecasts, and ICAT holds the calendar of the prefecture.

Then take the study's rows as your headings, since the useful part of it is the structure rather than the 2005 figures. Tell me how much land you have and whether you hire machinery, and I will tell you which rows apply to you.

But do one thing before the pegs go in: determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, because the layout is meant to follow the ground so the water circulates well over the whole plot. Two things to fix before you peg: check the plan is complete, with the slopes determined from your own measurements and the plan drawn from them, and remember that pegging in one line is the start of a sequence of pegs that build the bund. And remember the catalogue puts pegs in the building part rather than the water part, so a bund built with pegs is still a bund with a water channel built to carry it.

prompt.content: Describe a main bund to me as if I had cut through it.

Between the two, the height stands at 30 to 35 cm, so it comes up to about the middle of your shin. And along the run, towards each end, the wall is deliberately interrupted: those gaps are the spillways, provided to evacuate the excess water. prompt.content: True or false: ploughing and sowing happen in the same months.

chosen.content: In the brochure's bands they overlap, which is true but worth reading carefully. Ploughing is at the first rains: April and May in Maritime and Plateaux, June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Sowing is when the rains are properly settled: April to May in the south, June to July in the centre and north. So the months are the same, but the triggers are different, the first rains for one and settled rains for the other, and the order is fixed. What comes earlier is the clearing: February and March in the south, April and May in the centre and north.

rejected.content: False. In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, the plot is chosen in July, the sowing in April and May, the first weeding in June and July, and the second weeding in August and September. The brochure's own layout is a single season, in January and February for clearing, and March and April for the plot. In the north, Kara and Savanes, those are February and March for clearing and April and May for the plot, with clearing and ploughing at the same time. So the two practices belong to different calendars.

prompt.content: True or false: chicks and adults can share the same feeders.

chosen.content: False, and for two reasons the references give. The feeders are not the same size: a chick feeder is 50 cm by 50 by 5 and serves fifty chicks, an adult feeder is 150 cm by 12 by 16 and serves twenty-five birds. And the 2017 village compendium says plainly that young chicks must be fed apart from the adults, with their own special ration, and that it is better they do not compete with the adults for food. Chicks also need clean water badly, because they die easily of dehydration.

rejected.content: False. The 2017 ESFT compendium says chicks must be fed apart from adults so they do not have to compete, and it names the size as 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep for a chick feeder, while the 2019 village compendium says 12 by 10 by 6 for 60 chicks and 18 by 16 for 12 adults. Two reasons for the difference. The size difference is the same reason the compartment was built: it lets you watch feed and water closely, which is not as easily when the cocks and the chicks are mingling in the crowd. And the age difference comes from how the feed is used. The chick formula is 100 kg per 100 kg of feed, a third of what the adults eat, and it has less greenery, more mineral.

prompt.content: I am bringing home the sixty hens and six cocks tomorrow. What must be ready?

If any bird comes from a poultry market, the 2017 ESFT compendium says to hold it in quarantine for two weeks before it joins the rest. Plan a run around the henhouse so they do not wander: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one. Feeders, drinkers and nest boxes go inside. And open the four registers the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for: visits, movements, health follow-up, and money in and out.

rejected.content: Four things in particular. The housing: at least five compartments for the breeders, the brooding ones, where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are kept. The manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam. The feeders and drinkers you will wash and refill every day. And the handwork: sweeping the inside two or three times a week, because a floor swept daily holds 10,000 fleas and 20,000 ticks, and a bird that is not fed and waterless is a parasite problem of the whole flock.

And a brooder for the chicks, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, since the same study has a chick room of that size for 2,250 birds.

prompt.content: True or false: you should keep a breeding cock as long as he is alive.

chosen.content: False. Breeders are replaced. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference culls hens and cocks at 24 months; the 2017 ESFT compendium, which describes the village henhouse, culls the breeding cocks after three years of keeping. Both say to cull the breeders that no longer perform and the hens that do not lay. Renew either by selecting the best females among the young born on your farm, or by buying breeders from another region or a breeding centre.

rejected.content: False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping, whether they are alive or not. The cock decides whether the hens lay. If you want a hatching improvement, the 2017 ESFT compendium recommends six production cycles a year and culls the hens that no longer lay, in that order of culling. The 2018 village compendium says the same in its own terms: cull the breeding cocks after three years of keeping.

prompt.content: I am drawing up my henhouse plan and there are two things nobody can answer.

Tell me what they are. There are some things I can give you straight out of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference and some that reference genuinely does not contain, and it is worth knowing which is which before you go looking further.
Which way to face it, and what to put down for litter.

Everything else on your drawing I can help with: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, one with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding, a chick room with fewer openings so the warmth stays in, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard. Sizes from the densities, 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks, 12 to 15 for growers. Low wall 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, chick room walled higher with openings for air, tarpaulins for rain and wind. Outside, a grassy run, a store, and a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam. One note on litter while you wait for the answer: after changing it, and whenever there are lice, ticks or fleas, spray disinfectant inside the shelter.

rejected.content: I will answer both from what the reference does give. Its two compartments are divided by a shared wall, which it says lets you control the air you have inside, and its five compartments are defined by openings: one opened for the breeders at 2 m by 1.5 m, one for brooding, one for adults, one for a chick room, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard. The brooder is at 0.6 cubic metres for 60 chicks, and the chick room is at 0.5 cubic metres for 12 adults. Its own dimensions are 1.8 m by 1.2 m for a breeder compartment, 2 m by 1 m for a chick room, and 1.2 m by 1 m for a grower compartment, with a shared yard. Two things it does not give. prompt.content: Set out the pricing method and the market instructions.

chosen.content: The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference gives pricing as five steps: record every expense; work out the cost of production per head; decide the profit you want per head; compare that price with the market price; readjust if the market asks for it. On the market side it gives four instructions: look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after; keep a client register; sign contracts with them where you can; and honour what the contract says. Beside those it lists how to make the farm known: radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds, word of mouth and a signboard. The study names no buyer and gives no current price; its own figures, 2,250 FCFA a bird and 100 FCFA an egg, are 2020 evaluations used to build a projection.

rejected.content: Two things at once, because they are linked. The bird is the product, which is what the study is about: birds sold at six months for 2,250 FCFA. The way to get the birds to market. The first two weeks at 2,250 FCFA, 30 birds on a unit of 30. The second, 3,000 FCFA for six birds, at 60 grams a day from 1 to 60 days, with greenery, termites and maggots on top of the formula. The third, the whole point of the study: a unit sells 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA and 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA, so you can plan your own money in those terms before buying the farm equipment and the feed. Then look for your buyers before the batch starts rather than after, because the study sells after six months of keeping, at one hundred and ten birds per hundred eggs. And take the money in, which is why it matters: the study counts 2,376 eggs sold at 100 FCFA and 2,422 sold at 10,000 FCFA, on top of the 3,210,000 FCFA of start-up, in 2005 evaluations.

prompt.content: The money comes in but it all goes straight back out again.

chosen.content: That is what the first year looks like in the projection, and it is also what poor records look like, so separate the two. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 in year two, so very little left over is expected at this stage. But you should be able to see it rather than feel it: keep the registers that study asks for, visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out. Then set your price properly, which is its own instruction there: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare that with the market price and readjust. If after that the price you need is above what the market pays, that is a real answer and ICAT is where to take it.

rejected.content: That is the whole of the problem, and it is also the easy one to hide. The study's charges add up to 89,000 FCFA in 2005 evaluations and 77,000 in 2010 prices, so a small sum is a real sum in the budget. Tell the buyer what is there and ask him about the difference he is taking rather than about the price. If he wants a bigger margin, let him know the charges are a normal part of running an investment and that he should keep a small profit on the sale rather than expecting it.

prompt.content: Specify the layout stage.

chosen.content: Inputs: the slopes, determined with a water level; the plan of basins and drains, drawn from those slopes. Operation: mark the plan out on the site. Material: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare. Outputs to mark: the lines of the main bunds, which will be built 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high; the lines of the secondary bunds, 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30; and the spillway positions, towards the ends of the main bund. The catalogue gives no peg length, no spacing in metres and no cost.

rejected.content: The catalogue does not give one, and I will not invent one, because a wrong layout can cost you months of work. Its layout depends on the shape of the plot and on what you are actually going to plant: maize at 80 cm by 40 cm, or cowpea at 60 cm by 40 cm. What it does give on the next operation is how to do it. One rectangle for a single line, 80 cm by 40 cm, 4 m by 2 m, about 160 plants per hectare. One for a double line, 40 cm by 40 cm, about 20 m by 8 m, about 80 plants per hectare. Then the crop in the line: maize at the head, soya or cowpea in the lines, with a nitrogen-fixing plant between you and the main crop, a legume, and maize between two of those, which is what the alley cropping instruction is for. And the watering around it: water it well as you plant so the seedlings does not go down hard.

prompt.content: I have no money for five compartments at once. Which do I build first?

chosen.content: Start with what the birds you actually have need. The five compartments of the 2020 commercial reference are the breeders with a shared yard, the brooding room, the chick room, and two grower compartments with a yard. If you begin with a breeding nucleus of sixty hens and six cocks, the breeder compartment and the chick room come first, since chicks must be kept apart and warm. Build the rest as the flock grows, and ask ICAT to help you stage it against your budget.

rejected.content: The one the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks at the moment: the breeder compartment, the one with fewer openings, with fewer people inside it. It puts a breeder compartment at the rear of the breeder compartment, with its wall raised and left open for air, at 50 by 6.5 metres for 50 birds, inside a henhouse of 4 m by 3.5 m by 2 m, so 175 square metres for 550 birds. Build the rest as you can, at a lower floor, or leave the breeder compartment as a standalone. What does not cost money at this point is the ground: the 2017 ESFT compendium says the manure pit is at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, and gives no equipment for it, so you have to buy it.

prompt.content: Labour is free, my family works the field, so my charges are much lower.

chosen.content: The study counts family labour all the same, and that is deliberate. In the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare every operation is priced in man-days at 700 FCFA: 55 for harvest and transport, 30 for the first weeding and thinning, 30 for shelling and winnowing, 25 for the second weeding, and so on, in 2005 evaluations. Counting it shows you what your own time is worth in the result. You may choose not to pay it out, but leave it out of the budget and you will not know whether the crop really pays.

rejected.content: The study treats labour as 700 FCFA a day, in 2005 evaluations, and it counts it against the charge: the same rows give 391,000 FCFA of charges for 480 days, with 14,000 of them for man-days at 700 FCFA each. The difference you see is the difference between what the study sells and what you pay. Its profit of 89,000 FCFA on a yield of 3,500 kg assumes selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, and that is a 2005 evaluation. Your family working is the other side of the same equation: the study counts six bags a day at 20 FCFA each for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and its profit of 89,000 FCFA depends on selling after six months. So the two are not the same, they are two sides of the same thing.

prompt.content: My costs always come out higher than I planned.

chosen.content: Look at which rows you are leaving out of your plan, because the study counts several that people do not. prompt.content: Will the rains be good this year in the Plateaux?

chosen.content: I cannot know that. I am offline, I do not forecast, and only ANAMET issues forecasts and warnings in Togo. What I can tell you is the pattern: FAO GIEWS describes two rainy seasons in the south, around March to June and again around October. And the reason the question matters, which the calendar fiche states: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, which is why a sowing date is a guide and not a rule. Ask ANAMET for this season.

rejected.content: I cannot give a live forecast for this season. In the south, including Plateaux, rains come in two separate seasons each year. The northern zones like Kara and Savanes have one rainy period from roughly May to September. Centrale shows a mix of both patterns. To get an official forecast from ANAMET or ICAT, listen to the radio for any issued warnings. Prepare your planting plot ahead of time, taking into account the seasonal pattern. For turning that seasonal outlook into a planting timetable, you may consult ICAT.

prompt.content: My hens sit well and hatch well but I still end up with far fewer birds than I counted on.

chosen.content: Then look at the losses rather than at the hatching. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, and if your hatching is good the gap is in the second figure. Losing far more than one bird in ten is not the normal loss that model allows for. Watch for the signs it lists: the bird is sad, drowsy and downcast, its wings droop and its feathers stand up, it keeps away from the flock, it does not eat, it is thin, it has a discharge from the nose and the mouth, it moves with difficulty, and it has diarrhoea. Isolate any bird like that, take dead birds out fast and bury them well away, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Keep the movement register with hatchings and deaths so you can see where in the cycle you are losing them.

rejected.content: Counting hatchings is one thing and not the whole thing, so I want to be clear about which of the two I am talking about. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives an expected natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and it says that is what brings the output into the flock: 60 birds sold on the first year after hatchings counted and sold, at 25 to 30 grams a bird. So the first thing to do is check your eggs for what the reference counts and discard the ones that did not hatch. Then look at the sex ratio you set: one cock for ten hens, so for 60 hens you need about six cocks, and check the cock you have brought in, vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. Sell the birds that are still under six months rather than keeping them past the hatching point. If what you are still short of is chicks, that is a different question and worth separating from the hens; the brooder is what it needs for the first three weeks, 0.6 cubic metres of 0.6 m by 1 m by 50 cm high for 60 chicks. ICAT can look at both.

prompt.content: What does a bag of feed cost now?

chosen.content: I cannot tell you, and a figure invented here would go straight into your budget. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a total, 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in 2020 prices with feed as most of it, but it does not price a bag and those were 2020 evaluations in any case. What I can give you is the quantity, which is the part that does not move: from 1 to 60 days a bird eats about 1.5 kg in all at 10 to 25 grams a day, from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all at 25 to 35 grams a day, and a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day. Price those quantities at your own market, or ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal near you.

rejected.content: I cannot give a current price, and I will not build a projection on one. The method I am using is the 2,250,491 FCFA of 2005 evaluations for one unit, which is a 2005 evaluation and not a price today. Feed prices move with the season and with the market, and the study I am on carries no current input prices, no current seller, and no future projection. What the study does is show the structure of the unit in 2005, with feed as most of its 3,850,124 FCFA of first year working capital, and it is exactly where today's prices would sit. For today's, ask at an approved seller, or ask ICAT, which is the office for grain.

What comes later is the harvest side, the 55 man-days for harvest and transport, the 21,000 of jute bags, the 20,000 of pallets and the 14,000 of grain protectant. The brochure puts it first, at 20,000 FCFA of a 391,000 FCFA total in the 2008 maize brochure, which is why the costed hectare in the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure runs on it: 7,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea, 20,000 for the plot and 14,000 for the tractor pass. Then the tractor work, 40,000 for harvest and transport, 25,000 for the first weeding and thinning, 20,000 for shelling and winnowing, 10,000 for treatment and bagging, 2,000 for the plot and 20,000 for the seed. prompt.content: A women's group in my village wants to start keeping hens and they asked where to buy.

chosen.content: Point them at a well followed farm or a research centre rather than at the poultry market, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for, and tell them what to look at: birds vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock at six months. Tell them the numbers too, because groups usually buy badly: one cock for about ten hens, and 60 hens and 6 cocks if they mean to run it as a commercial unit. And tell them the quarantine, two weeks for every bird before it joins whatever they already keep, bought or given. ICAT is the one to ask about what is available near them; I cannot name a supplier or quote a price.

rejected.content: Tell them the three places to buy are CAGIA or its authorized distributors, or a cooperative through its member shops. Give them the nine things the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks when buying input, which are products published by them, including the commercial varieties. Tell them to ask ICAT for the list of approved distributors near you, and ask them whether the product they are looking for is still covered by the outlet they picked. And tell them the study is right at the bottom of the brochure's table of contents, so they know it is part of the reference they are following. ICAT itself is also where they can help with the business side, which is worth pointing out.

prompt.content: Set out the construction procedure.

chosen.content: Before construction: determine the slopes with a water level; draw the plan from them; mark the plan out on the site with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare. Construction: raise the bunds to profile, main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30; water them as they are built so that they compact. Openings: leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund to let excess water out. Organisation: the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation. Site: replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site.

rejected.content: Cut the vegetative components first, since the catalogue says that is where the rest of the improvement goes: jatropha and theppia are sown on top of the soil for that purpose. Take the deep, well drained soil, or a trench 50 cm wide and 20 cm deep for the maize, since the catalogue says to do it in rows 80 cm apart. Then leave the residues of last season out, because the catalogue calls them the material to improve. Then the trees themselves, which it names as the first step in the improved continuation: teak, gmelina, which it also calls Indian teak, leucaena, acacia, senna and neem, the latter used as the weedicide. Then the watering, since the catalogue says to water the seedlings for the first weeks. Then the laying of the low wall, 0.5 to 1 m, and of the high banks, 30 to 40 cm high. And then the finishing, which is the part most people leave out: spreading wood ash on the inside of the trench, watering it well and leaving it, so as to have a nutrient bed.

prompt.content: How tall will the hedge get and how long before it holds animals?

chosen.content: Neither is in the catalogue and I will not guess at them, since you would plan your fencing around the answer. What it gives is the trench, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line or 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line; the three ways of planting, direct sowing, cuttings or potted plants; jatropha and thevetia as species often used between the trees; and the aftercare, weeding and replacing dead plants for the two following seasons. It gives no height, no growth time and no cost. That aftercare period is the only time figure it offers. Ask ICAT for the rest.

prompt.content: How do I prepare for a season that starts late?

chosen.content: Choose the cycle against the season you have left rather than the calendar date. The maize brochure ties a cycle to timing in one place, the maize then cotton succession in the same year, where it says to sow an extra early variety of 75 to 85 days. Improved varieties of that length exist in the list of nine released in Togo. Avoid late sowing in any case, since maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south and late sowings in the north. Ask ANAMET for this year's rains.

rejected.content: Choose the variety at the start of the season rather than late, since the released list runs from 75 to 85 days at the short end up to 105 to 115 days at the long. Knowing your prefecture's rains is also part of the plan: the useful rains run roughly May to September, and a second one is not something to count on as an extra. The brochure's own word is maize streak virus does its damage mainly on late sowings in the south, which is why a late sowing is a risk to put into consideration. And if you are sowing after a previous crop, the rule is the same, the improved varieties released in Togo are all tolerant to maize streak virus.

prompt.content: Everything on my farm is the same age and the henhouse is empty half the year.

chosen.content: You are running one cycle where the model runs six. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year, which is why it asks for at least five compartments: a breeder compartment, a brooding compartment, a chick room and two grower compartments, all occupied at once by birds of different ages. Start staggering: set a batch of eggs, then another before the first leaves the brooder at three weeks, and so on. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs, and the brooder is meant to handle small hatchings in series, so the equipment already assumes this. Staggering also spreads your sales, which matters because you are meant to find buyers before each batch is ready. Write the settings and hatchings in the movement register so you can see the rhythm build.

The 2023 ESFT compendium is from a second time and says the same: a commercial unit of local hens should hatch for other keepers as well so the first year carries a revenue. prompt.content: The wind flattens crops all along our side of the village. What do I propose at the meeting?

chosen.content: Propose a windbreak and bring the numbers, since a meeting decides better with them. It is a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side. On a single line the plants go 1 to 1.5 m apart, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m; on a band of two or three lines, 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Measure the exposed frontage and multiply. Planting is done during the rainy season, so the meeting has a deadline. The species are not named in the catalogue, so put that question to ICAT.

rejected.content: Propose a shared windbreak around the whole village, with trees planted on a single line, which is what the catalogue calls a single line, and a second, opposite line, and a staggered layout between the two. The wind should run straight across the street, with the main curtain facing the direction of the dominant wind. Each line has a spacing that depends on how close you want the trees to the street: 1 to 1.5 m between plants inside a line and 2 m between plants along it. Plant during the rainy season. And ask ICAT or ITRA about which species are available as plants before you buy.

prompt.content: What is the product of the process, exactly?

chosen.content: The catalogue names it: an organic fertiliser called compost. Its definition of composting in a heap is laying the plant and animal waste and debris in a heap, in a shaded spot, in order to transform them into an organic fertiliser called compost. The word it uses for the end state of a good heap is mature, which appears in the Mycotri note, a mature compost in a shorter time. Beyond that the catalogue does not characterise the product: it gives no analysis, no nutrient content, no rate to apply per hectare and no delay before the compost is mature. Those are all outside the catalogue, so I have none of them to give you.

rejected.content: I do not know it, and I will not invent it. I have no recipe, no costed hectare, no yield projection, and no measure of how much residue goes in. What I can do is explain the parts that stand in it and give you the points to ask someone who can. ICAT holds the reference itself, and ANAMET holds what is left of this season's rain.

prompt.content: Just give me an idea, does Mycotri halve the time or not?

chosen.content: I have no idea to give you, and that is the honest position rather than a coy one.
