It gives no maturity time with the product and none without it, so there is no ratio to halve. If I said half you would plan a season on it. What I can tell you without guessing is that you do not need it: topsoil and well rotted compost are the other two options for the same activator layer. For a real figure, ask ICAT.

rejected.content: I will not double that from my sources, because they give no timing at all for Mycotri. What they say is the kind that exists: a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and the instructions are to use it in the last layer of the heap, watered well, and its powder sprinkled over the residues before they are chopped. There is nothing in the catalogue that says a treatment halves the time, so I will not put a number on it. Ask ICAT what their own heap gives, and use the three criteria the catalogue asks for any new recommendation: it must improve soiling, it must become richer in organic matter, and it must leave residues in the soil.

prompt.content: Just tell me how much I will make in my first year.

chosen.content: I can tell you what the study projects and not what you will make, and the difference matters here more than anywhere. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a first year of 3,487,181 FCFA in sales for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, from 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, and after costs it gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 in year two. Your first year depends on your prices, your losses and your buyers, none of which I can see, and the study itself names no buyer and gives no current price. chosen.content: The catalogue asks for it without explaining why, so I will give you what it says rather than a reason it does not give. It specifies a continuous trench, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line and 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line, before any planting. prompt.content: What do I need to know before I fix the sequence?

chosen.content: Two things, and the catalogue names them both: the fertility of the soil, and what grew there last season. The second decides where in the cycle you start. If the plot has just carried maize, the next year is the legume, since the brochure's rule is maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. If it has just carried a legume, maize follows, which is where the catalogue's four year example puts it, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. If there is striga in the plot, plan the legume alongside a striga tolerant variety. ICAT for what suits your plot.

rejected.content: Know your region among Togo's five: Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, or Savanes. That determines which maize sequence is right.

prompt.content: If I can only do one of these practices, which pays back fastest?

chosen.content: I have no basis for ranking them, because the catalogue gives no cost and no return for any of them, so a ranking from me would be invention dressed as advice. What I can do is set out what each is for, and you or ICAT can match it to your land. Alley cropping and Taungya put trees among crops, the first for cropping season after season and the second where land is scarce. A windbreak is for wind coming across an exposed field. A live hedge is for keeping animals, wind or light out. Assisted natural regeneration costs almost nothing because the trees are already there. Composting is for soil fertility. Lowland development is for rice water.

rejected.content: I cannot rank them by yield, because the catalogue does not, so I will not claim that. Then there is the land for it.

prompt.content: It has rained twice this week in the Plateaux and I am tempted to put the seed in.

chosen.content: Two rains in a week is closer to settled than one shower, but the test is regularity rather than a count, and the brochure puts it as sowing when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, with a warning not to sow on one isolated shower. You are in the right band for Maritime and Plateaux, where sowing goes in April to May, so the calendar is not against you. If you are in Kara or Savanes in the north, sow at the start of the reliable rains, around March to April, and have the plot ready to sow as soon as they start. After sowing, have the plot clear of residues from the last season, because the guidance is to keep crop residues in the soil, so leave or bury what you planted this season.

prompt.content: I want to put fertiliser trees into my maize field.

Then alley cropping is the practice, and I need two things to give you a layout: which way the land slopes, and how wide you want the cropped strips. The catalogue is firm on the first, the alleys go across the slope and not down it, and offers a choice on the second, 10, 20 or 30 m between one tree row and the next.
It slopes gently to the west, and I want the strips wide enough to work with the oxen.

chosen.content: Then run your rows north and south, across that westward slope, and take the widest spacing, 30 m between one row and the next, which leaves you strips you can work without turning constantly. Inside each row, space the plants 2 to 4 m apart. Grow your maize in the alleys, or cowpea, which are the two the catalogue names. Plant the trees during the rainy season. The three fertiliser trees it names are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, which it describes as a fertilising plant resistant to drought, and Faidherbia albida; ask ICAT which is available as plants near you. Then hold one date in mind from the start: the first pruning comes between 15 and 20 months, when the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, and a high cut at 2 m above the ground is advised. After that you prune regularly, and what you cut is firewood or organic fertiliser for the field.

rejected.content: Then the spacing on the 10 m side is 7.5 to 10 m. The catalogue sets the spacing first for a stand of trees, 12 to 15 adult trees per hectare and 30 to 45 young shoots per hectare; it does not say how many you will plant in a row, nor how many you will run across a field, nor how much you will set to one hectare. So that is your spacing and you should take it to ICAT. What I can put to you on the crop is the fertiliser component: you plant the trees in March, with the rows set 1 to 1.5 m apart for species such as Leucaena leucocephala, or 2 m between the rows and 1.5 m within the row for Senna siamea, and replant the trees after ten years.

prompt.content: What do I bring to ICAT to build my own budget?

Your labour operation by operation, in days: sowing, spreading NPK, the first weeding and thinning, the urea, the second weeding, harvest and transport, drying, shelling and winnowing, treatment and bagging. And the small items you actually buy: grain protectant, jute bags, pallets, twine and needle. Then the prices you pay today. That is a budget rather than a wish.

Tell me whether you are planting maize, sorghum, millet or maize with or without cowpea, and whether you are with or without a second crop. Tell me the number of days your rains run under, that is how much of the season they are actually there. Tell me whether you are buying seeds, fertiliser, tractor ploughing or other work from outside. And tell me which of the three bags of NPK, urea or fungicide you use.

When you do cut, the catalogue advises going to 2 m above the ground, which it calls a high cut. After that first one, the prunings become regular, and their rhythm depends on the kind of tree you planted, on how it grows, and on what you want from it, firewood or organic fertiliser.

rejected.content: Then you are within the period the catalogue advises for first pruning, which is between 15 and 30 months, and it will get worse if you start earlier. Cut the trees at 1.50 m above the ground, which is what the 12,000 FCFA of plant material is for. What you are doing now is the part where you will hurt the growth: the first pruning is carried out between 15 and 30 months, which is when the trees stand at the age at which you would want a high yield. If you want a different answer for that time, that is a question for the planting itself, which is what the catalogue offers: a windbreak at 1 to 1.5 m by 2 m, the trees chosen in that order are Leucaena, Senna or Faidherbia albida, and the alleys laid out with trays for the large trees.

prompt.content: Should I build one big room or separate compartments?

chosen.content: Separate compartments, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for at least five: one with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are hatched, a chick room, and two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. The reason is in the densities: breeders at 8 to 10 per square metre, chicks at 50, growers at 12 to 15. One room cannot hold three densities, and the chick room in particular has fewer openings than the others so the warmth stays in. Plan two more things beside the henhouse, a grassy run and a store. For the plans themselves, ICAT.

rejected.content: The compartmentalized breeder room is the one the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for, at least 4 cubic metres, with a floor of 0.6 to 1 m by 1.2 to 1 m high. It is the compartment the reference recommends for keeping the chicks warm, and it puts the chick room within reach of the henhouse so she can watch them. The 2017 compendium asks for at least five compartments in the commercial unit: two adult rooms for the breeders, one for brooding, a chick room and a pusiller for the illness. If your birds are small, take the reference's one room and the brooding compartment out to two, or split the two in half rather than putting one together.

prompt.content: What does the reference specify about acquiring the breeding stock?

chosen.content: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies the source, the selection and the size. Source: a well followed farm or a research centre. Selection: birds vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb; at six months about 1.3 kg live weight for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Size: a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, at one cock for ten hens, and those birds are among the items counted in its start-up evaluation of 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, alongside the houses, the store, the manure pit, the gas incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders, the drinkers and the nests. The separation rule applies to all of them: two weeks of quarantine before any new bird joins the flock.

rejected.content: From the 2017 ESFT compendium, which is the one that sets out how to build the breeding nucleus: it advises gathering breeders from your own village or from among the best local breeders, and names the criteria, the vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, the good layers, chosen from a well followed farm or a research centre, the one cock being about 1.5 kg for a hen and about 1.3 kg for a cock. It also names the cost of the birds, at six tons for 60 hens and six cocks, alongside the money for the housing, the feed and the health. And it puts the whole thing in the same breath as the next stage: breeding for a good number of offspring, because a nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks is 66 birds, at one cock for ten hens.

prompt.content: I read somewhere that a hectare of maize costs about 72,000 FCFA. Is that the whole cost?

chosen.content: No, that is one line inside the budget and not the bottom of it. In the 2005 evaluation published by ITRA and ICAT the charges for one hectare of Obatanpa maize add up to 391,000 FCFA in total, and the crop sells for 480,000 FCFA, leaving 89,000 FCFA of profit on 3,500 kg per hectare. A single item is easy to mistake for the total because it is the one people quote, and a budget built on it would leave you short by a wide margin. Work from the total and check which items your own plot actually needs.

rejected.content: The study counts 72,000 FCFA of input but does not count the machine work, so the total cost of 391,000 FCFA is the input plus the labour, and you do not see the labour in its figures. What the study does show is the yield, a hectare gives 3,500 kg, and it projects a sale of 1,422 kg at 2,250 FCFA per bag, so the profit is 391,000 FCFA of that 2,250 FCFA. The study also projects a year of 3,487,181 FCFA of charges and 2,376,500 FCFA of sales, and it is the whole of it that will pay back on the loan it asks for. For the cost of the land, the plots, the tractor ploughing, the pulverising pass, the seed, the fertiliser and the workers, get their own rows. Take the profit figure and the rows to ICAT for the complete cost of production.

prompt.content: Describe how the work falls across the season.

chosen.content: It comes in three bunches. At the start, small: 10 man-days for sowing, then 20 for spreading NPK. In the middle, the weeding: 30 days for the first weeding and thinning and 25 for the second, with 10 for the urea between them. At the end, the heaviest stretch: 55 days for harvest and transport, then 10 for drying, 30 for shelling and winnowing and 20 for treatment and bagging. So more than half of those 210 days fall after the crop is cut, which is the part people underestimate. All priced at 700 FCFA a day in the study, 2005 prices.

rejected.content: The catalogue divides it into two seasons. In the first the work consists of ploughing at the first rains, clearing the plot, and of the first weeding and of sowing when the rains are settled, at the first rains. In the second the work consists of building the heap, the residues trodden down, watering each layer as you lay it down, and of the second the residues are what carries the whole thing on, not the work itself. And there is a third type of work in the middle, the carrying out of the work carried out in the second season, which is the clearing of the fallow, the pruning of the trees, the removal of Striga, the stocking and the health measures. The whole of it is carried out in the main season, from June to August.

rejected.content: It is a series of alternating phases, not a single block. In April and May the clearing is done, and the ploughing is done at the first rains, in June and July. Then the first harvest is the main one, in October, when the rains are settled, and the second is the second one, in January and February. Between these two, you are ploughing and sowing, and you are also weeding, drying the crop and moving the harvested stalks up into the bags. Each operation is a different task, and the intervals between them matter because the crop needs moisture to move on from one bag to the next.

prompt.content: I am thinking about buying an incubator.

Tell me how many breeding hens you keep, because the sizing in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference runs from the flock: a gas incubator of 300 eggs suits 60 breeding hens. And tell me whether there is anyone else near you who hatches, because that reference attaches a condition to the purchase.
Forty hens, and there are two or three other keepers in the village.

chosen.content: Then you are under the flock the 300 egg machine is sized for, and the other keepers are the thing that makes it work anyway. The reference says that even at 60 hens you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself, so at 40 that is not an extra, it is the plan. Go and agree it with those two or three before you buy, and agree what you charge, using the same method the reference gives for pricing anything: record every expense, work out the cost per unit, decide the profit you want, compare with what people will pay, readjust. Meanwhile your hens can hatch, twelve to fourteen eggs each over twenty-one days, which is the same incubation the machine gives. And remember that with machine-hatched chicks there is no mother hen, so the brooder becomes compulsory: 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, covering their first three weeks. Take the whole calculation to ICAT.

rejected.content: Then buy one or two of them, and buy it now rather than in the future. The reference sizes the gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens at 25 to 32 eggs each, and a larger machine than that is not worth the lead time you will have to wait for it. If you do buy more, put your two or three other keepers together, because the same reference says a cooperative is the way to sell together. If they are not, the reference stops there and tells you to hatch for another keeper or at the village compound, which is usually worse, and not to buy the machine at all. Take the number of hens to ICAT before you buy, which is the office for the model that matches the unit to your flock.

prompt.content: Just tell me something I can sow in October, anything.

chosen.content: I will not name a crop, and this is one of the clearest cases where an invented answer would cost you real money. None of my sources says which crop to sow in a given month such as October, and I have no cycle figures for anything but maize. What I can tell you about October is only the shape: FAO GIEWS puts a second rainy season in the south around that time, and the northern season running around May to October. If you are in the south and thinking of a second maize crop, the plot for it is chosen in July and it needs an improved tolerant variety. For an actual crop, ICAT, and ANAMET for the rains.

rejected.content: I will not name a crop, and naming one would send you toward a year you do not have. The source I hold is the calendar of the country it was taken from, which runs from 55 to 75 days for the main season to 105 to 115 for a second season, and it does not split those for October at all. What I can point at is the constraint rather than the answer. What sows in October in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, is not a single crop, it is maize with cassava, cowpea, groundnut or a combination, and the brochure's own words are that those are the crops sown there for October and November. For a crop for a different region, ask ICAT.

prompt.content: How do I choose which eggs to put under the hen?

chosen.content: Collect the eggs every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry. Then sort them and throw out the ones that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked, or that have no pointed end. Keep them seven to ten days at most before setting them, and set them pointed end down. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs. Expect a hatching rate near seventy percent, which is the figure the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on.

rejected.content: Keep them seven to ten days at most. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to keep the eggs seven to ten days before setting them, and that is the warm, dry, airy, sealed ones where the keets are. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says the same thing in the same order: collect the eggs, sort them, keep them seven to ten days where keets are in the brooder, and set them pointed end down. So a brooder is used as a stand-in for the eggs that are meant to go there.

prompt.content: Just tell me I can skip the pallets, the floor is dry enough.

chosen.content: I will not tell you to skip them, because the storage is what the study's profit rests on. It sells after six months at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, and the brochure's own sentence is that a maize kept on treated pallets in an airy store holds six months without weevil attack. Take the pallets out and you are storing differently from the study whose profit you are planning on. They are 20,000 FCFA of a 391,000 FCFA charge, against a profit of 89,000. If a dry floor really does as well, that is worth asking ICAT, but I am not the one who can tell you so.

rejected.content: I will not, because the catalogue's instruction is the opposite: use a rammed or composite building material, and leave the structures sturdy and well maintained. A floor that is dry is not the reason you are skipping the pallets, it is the reason it is not a substitute. The 2017 ESFT compendium asks for a store that protects the granary from animals and the weather, so a dry floor is part of the same protection. If you are not yet at the store, the pallets are not a substitute either: they are for the storage part of the henhouse, not for keeping a whole building.

prompt.content: I want to plan my year so the birds are ready for the big market days.

chosen.content: Then count backwards from the sale, because the cycle length is fixed. Birds are sold at six months, when a hen weighs about 1.3 kg and a cock about 1.5 kg, so a bird you want ready in September was an egg set in about March. The incubation is twenty-one days, the brooder covers the first three weeks, then the chick room, then the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year, so you have room to stagger the settings rather than hatching everything at once. Two things it asks you to do alongside: look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after, and keep a movement register of sales, hatchings and deaths so you can see the pattern next year.

rejected.content: Then start from where the study is built: the unit starts at 2,250 FCFA a bird and sells for 1,200 FCFA, and sells after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA, on top of a first year selling 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA and 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA. So the whole point of the storage is to hold the birds for two seasons. Tell me what you can afford to spend on the store first, and I will show you the arithmetic.

It explains the difference by the larger number of birds sold in year two and by the fall in financial charges. Treat both as evaluations for one unit, not as what you will earn, and check any price you plan on against your own market.

The same study also plans on three more years of net first year income at 2,790,400 FCFA in year two and 3,487,000 in year three. prompt.content: I have nowhere to store and a trader is offering to take the lot at harvest.

chosen.content: Then you are not in the study's case, and you should know what that changes. Its profit of 89,000 FCFA on the hectare comes from selling after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, on the brochure's reasoning that keeping the maize six months lets you sell it dearer when the time comes. Selling at harvest is selling into the glut. Two things to do. Work out your cost per bag from your own rows and compare it with what he is offering, so you know your floor. And follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio to see how the two moments compare. For the store itself, ICAT.

rejected.content: Then the two problems are not in my training and both are worth treating. For the grain, the brochure asks you to store it well dried, and it names two places where the brochure does say grain is kept: a fenced henhouse and a henhouse with a grassy run, and it adds that a henhouse should be located near your home rather than in the market area. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a turnout option alongside the henhouse one, and it adds that keeping birds near your home also lets you sell the droppings. So the first is a fenced run around the henhouse with a grassy run beside it, and the second is keeping the birds near home rather than at a market. Buy the lot from an approved seller, which is what the study asks you to do before handling a granary. ICAT holds the reference.

prompt.content: My rains usually run about ninety days and I want the most I can get.

chosen.content: Then the varieties that fit your season are the ones at 90 to 95 and 90 to 100 days, and among those the best yielder on the list is Ikenne 9449 SR, 90 to 100 days, 5 tonnes a hectare potential and 2 to 3.5 on average, which the brochure also marks as very steady in yield. Beside it sit Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen at 90 to 95 days and AB11 at 90 to 100, all at 4 tonnes potential and 2 to 3 on average. Going longer would mean Obatanpa at 100 to 110 days, which is more than ninety. Check with ICAT or ITRA that it suits your region this season, and buy from an approved seller.

rejected.content: Then sow at the start of the reliable rains, not on a first shower, and have your plot ready before they arrive. The rule I put to it is this: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. If you cannot wait for a long stretch, plant a short season variety such as TZEE W Pop STR QPM or EV99 QPM, both of which are marked as tolerant to short rains, and get the two sown together with or in addition to each other, since the brochure says a short season variety is sown from January to May in that country.

prompt.content: What good is a brooder if I already have broody hens?

chosen.content: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives four things it buys you. It saves the fuel you would spend heating the chicks. It handles small hatchings coming one after another. It keeps predators off the chicks. And it lets you watch their feeding and their health closely. A brooding hen does the warmth part well, and the 2017 village compendium says she adjusts it by the chicks' cries, but she takes only twelve to fourteen eggs at a time.

rejected.content: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names brooders as equipment you buy outright, not something to use when you already have birds. Its instruction is to build the chick room, which includes a chick feeder and drinker with room for twenty birds at most, so you do not need the brooder for every newly hatched bird. But it gives two reasons for the brooder: the brooder handles small hatchings in series so you do not have to hatch out several chicks at once, and it keeps the chicks warm. The 2017 ESFT compendium goes further, and names its own material: 0.6 cubic metres of banco at 80 cm by 40 by 20 for 60 chicks, 3.5 m long and 2 m wide and 1 m deep, which is enough if you hatch naturally. So a brooder is useful in its own right, and not a replacement for the chicks you already have.

prompt.content: Should I sell the droppings or put them on my own maize?

chosen.content: Both are in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it depends on whether you have fields of your own. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the pit two purposes, and the first is to turn the droppings into something your fields can use; the droppings then fertilise those fields. On the other side, its first year projection counts 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA in 2020 prices among the three things the unit sells, with 1,422 birds and 2,376 eggs. So if you crop, using them is a saved cost rather than a lost sale; if you do not, they are a third product you would otherwise throw away. Either way the pit is the same: at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam, well away from the henhouse.

rejected.content: You decide after two calculations, and the study gives you the arithmetic. The first is the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, which evaluates the unit at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices for 60 hens and 6 cocks, and it gives the first year projection of 3,487,181 FCFA in sales, based on 1,422 birds, 2,376 eggs and 50 kg of droppings. The second is the 2017 ESFT compendium, which evaluates the unit at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices and projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one. Those are 2020 evaluations, not today's prices, and they tell you whether the unit will pay for itself. What to do with the droppings: they go into the 50 kg of droppings at 20 FCFA a kg, so 6,500 kg in a year, which is not much. Rebuild the projection with today's prices.

prompt.content: I always seem to be either overrun with birds or with none to sell.

chosen.content: That is a staggering problem rather than a flock problem. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year and houses several ages at once, in at least five compartments, so that something is always coming to sale age. Set eggs in smaller batches more often: a brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen, the incubation is twenty-one days, the brooder covers the first three weeks and is meant to handle small hatchings in series, and sale comes at six months. Pair that with the selling instruction, which is to look for your buyers before the batch starts rather than after, with a client register and contracts where you can. The movement register, with sales, hatchings and deaths, is what will show you the gaps before you feel them.

rejected.content: The second figure in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference is 1,422 birds sold at 2,250 FCFA and 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA, in 2020 prices, and the net result is a profit of 2,376,000 FCFA against 3,487,181 FCFA in 2020 sales, so overrunning by a factor of about 2.7 is what you are describing. Work out your own prices in the same reference and compare them with what people are asking today, which is what the study is built around. Keep the movement register: sales, hatchings and deaths, and compare against what you charged.

prompt.content: amenagement simple bas-fond c'est quoi

chosen.content: Building basins and drains so that the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. The sequence: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, mark it out with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, then raise the bunds to profile, watering them as you build so they compact, leaving spillways towards the ends of the main bund. The catalogue advises doing the work as a group through a farmers' organisation.

rejected.content: Building basins and drains so the water moves properly over the whole plot. Steps: Know the slopes with a water level; draw basins and drains so water flows evenly over the whole plot. Main bund: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, so 115 to 150 cm total. Secondary bund: 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 cm at the top, 25 to 30 cm high, so 105 to 150 cm total. The plan is drawn from the slopes recorded with a water level. Do it as a group with your community to save time and money. After the plot is watered, stakes are used to check the shape of the bunds. For a specific practice adapted to your crop, see ICAT.
